display_title: Official Review of Submission7235 by Reviewer Xy2v

summary.value: The paper introduces AIMS.AU, a new benchmark containing 5,731 corporate modern slavery statements for LLMs to assess whether they meet the requirements of the Australian Modern Slavery Act. It details the construction and annotation process. The author benchmarks it over both fine-tuned open (BERT, DistilBERT, Llama2) and closed (GPT3.5-turbo, GPT4o) LLMs and finds zero-shot prompting LLM’s results aren’t comparable to fine-tuned LLMs, indicating dataset’s usage to fill the gap in corporate compliance analysis.

strengths.value:
1. The coverage of the dataset is extensive in terms of year and corporate entity (covering 7,270 entities’ statements from 2019 to 2023 after the establishment of Australian Modern Slavery Act). 

2. The dataset focuses on a specific field that could have significant social impact (but limited to Australia as generalizability is not shown) as it manages to enhance LLMs ability to assess modern slavery countermeasures in corporate statements.

weaknesses.value:
1. The presentation of this paper is subpar. It relies too much on text and does not take advantage of tables or figures. Some important information is either missing or in the Appendix instead of the main paper. See detailed comments in the "Questions" section below. 

2. Experiments are limited (order in priority). 
   - It only includes closed LLM in the setting of zero-shot prompting LLMs. The comparison between zero-shot open LLM and fine-tuned open LLM is interesting to see.

   - Few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting are missing. Closed instruction finetuned LLMs takes advantage of prompting techniques. It would be interesting to see how much improvement they will make using these two prompt fashions.

   - It only includes Llama-2-7b. Comparison between different size open-weight LLMs before and after fine-tuning is interesting to see.

   - Not benchmark the recent open-weight LLMs (like Llama-3)

3. The broad impact of this dataset is limited. The criteria for LLMs to identify is very specific to the Australia Modern Slavery Act. Can the learnings be transferred to "UK Modern Slavery Act 2015" which is similar? 

4. Benchmark task doesn’t take full advantage of the dataset. The author can formulate a better task to benchmark LLMs or VLMs. There is image information in the dataset which could potentially contribute to classification accuracy.

questions.value:
1. Typos in line 174: “CCalifornia” --> “California”

2. A figure depicting the annotation process would be helpful and easier to follow and understand.

3. I suggest putting Section3: related works in the later part of the paper so that important sections (Dataset Description and Benchmark Experiments) will come earlier.

4. The temperature of LLMs is not reported. 

5. Llama-2's size, which is important, is not revealed in the main paper. 

6. The regular expressions to convert text into sentences and extract LLMs’ responses are not revealed.

confidence.description: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

While chain-of-thought prompting is indeed an exciting and promising approach, we consider it an avenue for future exploration beyond the scope of the current work, which is focusing on providing a dataset and an initial benchmark. 

4/ We added Llama3.2 3B model to allow a comparison against Llama2 7B. Results showcase improvements in Llama3.2 3B in the fine-tuned case.

5/ We added Llama3.2 3B to the reported results.

6/ Thank you for this important question regarding the UK Modern Slavery Act. We updated the last paragraph of the Background Section for more clarity. However, we would like to respectfully emphasize that the generalizability of our dataset and approach to other jurisdictions, including the UK Modern Slavery Act of 2015, has been clearly addressed in our manuscript.  The last paragraph of the Background Section and “Comparison of Modern Slavery Reporting Criteria and Metrics” Appendix, in particular, highlight that the dataset is designed to be generalizable beyond the specific context of the Australian Modern Slavery Act. Furthermore, the table in the same Appendix demonstrates the potential for knowledge transfer across jurisdictions. This visualization illustrates how the criteria identified by our model can be applied to legislation with similar frameworks, such as the UK Modern Slavery Act. We believe that the methodologies developed in this work are adaptable and can serve as a foundation for analyzing similar legal frameworks in other regions, thus significantly extending the impact of our research.

7/ While we recognize the potential of incorporating vision-language models (VLMs) in future work, the focus of this paper is on introducing the dataset and establishing a benchmark centered on the textual components. Our primary goal is to provide a foundation for evaluating language models (LLMs), which we believe is a critical first step in understanding the dataset's utility. Expanding the benchmark to include VLMs would indeed be valuable, but it falls outside the scope of this paper. Such experiments would require additional resources and infrastructure beyond our current capacity, as well as a shift in focus from our initial goal of enabling researchers to explore the dataset and its linguistic aspects. We are confident that the provided benchmark will serve as a strong starting point for future research, including multimodal approaches.

8/ Typo fixed.

10/ We have taken your suggestions to shorten the Related Works Section into account and relocated the Related Works Section to precede the Conclusion Section. title.value: # Transferability of the AIMS.au Dataset to UK Statements

comment.value:
Thank you very much for your revised score and for your suggestions, helping us shape a stronger and more refined paper. 

To answer your question about the fine-tuned model on AIMS.au performance on other datasets, particularly in contexts where reporting criteria overlap, we conducted a preliminary experiment by annotating 10 UK documents and applying our model trained on the AIMS.au dataset. The results are as follows:

| **Metric/Category**      | **F1 Score** | **Precision** | **Recall** |
|--------------------------|-------------|---------------|------------|
| **Macro Average**        | 0.461844    | 0.55474       | 0.491747   |
| **Approval**             | 0.857143    | 0.75          | 1          |
| **Signature**            | 0.689655    | 1             | 0.526316   |
| **C2 (Structure)**       | 0.37037     | 0.454545      | 0.3125     |
| **C2 (Operations)**      | 0.634921    | 0.588235      | 0.689655   |
| **C2 (Supply Chains)**   | 0.628571    | 0.785714      | 0.52381    |
| **C3 (Risk Description)**| 0.166667    | 0.090909      | 1          |
| **C4 (Risk Mitigation)** | 0.609053    | 0.770833      | 0.503401   |
| **C4 (Remediation)**     | 0.5625      | 0.9           | 0.409091   |
| **C5 (Effectiveness)**   | 0.561404    | 0.761905      | 0.444444   |


### Performance
- While the overall performance was lower compared to Australian statements, the model demonstrated meaningful signals in several categories, such as **“Approval”**, **"C2 (Operations)"**, and **"C4 (Risk Mitigation)"**.
- Categories like **"C3 (Risk Description)"** showed limited performance, likely due to the scarcity of relevant instances in these UK documents (e.g., only 1 out of 10 statements described risks).

### Dataset Limitations
1. **Size**: The experiment was conducted on a small sample of 10 annotated UK documents, limiting the robustness of the results.
2. **Annotation Quality**: Quick turnaround and the absence of double-validation processes may have impacted annotation consistency.

## Future Directions
We plan to address this critical aspect as part of our future work. Specifically, we are planning on exploring the model’s transferability to the UK and Canadian contexts. These efforts will be integral to our upcoming research and publications, aimed at expanding the model's applicability to support Modern Slavery reporting checks across diverse regulatory frameworks.

We hope this demonstrates the potential of models trained on the AIMS.au dataset to perform effectively on other datasets and highlights the dataset's broader utility. 

We would be delighted to answer any further questions you may have.

summary.value: The paper describes an approach to construct a manually annotated dataset for modern slavery countermeasures detection and analysis in text based in Australia.  It also benchmarks modern language models including SLMs and LLMs in  zero-shot and supervised learning settings.

strengths.value:
-	The paper is clearly written and well-organized
-	The targeted domain/problem is unique yet very important and the proposed approach can be extended to other similar/relevant use cases
-	Experiments cover variety of setups, different types of SLMs and LLMs and with fine-tuning.

weaknesses.value:
-	I think more justifications to decisions made in proposed approach are needed:
        
	-	Line 238 – 242: more discussion and justifications are needed to explain the need for such different subsetting and annotation approaches. 
	-	Please justify/further discuss the quality of the OCR tools used.
-	Since the dataset is the main contribution of the work, details on its annotation process should be moved to main text. For example:

	-	11 questions are mentioned in paragraph starting from line 285, examples of these questions and potential answers should be added in main text. 

	-	In line 305 ++ it isn’t enough to mention a company did the annotation. What are the characteristics of annotators (other than being fluent English speakers)? How was training exactly done? these are core details to establish dataset quality.
	-	How was the dataset split for train and test?

questions.value:
-	Related work can be shortened, the paper is already covering both an introduction and background (around half of the paper is just introductory pages). This is especially important given that most related work isn’t specifically targeting the exact problem at hand.
-	Did you annotate all statements/docs mentioned starting from line 250? 
-	I suggest better formatting and maybe a figure to describe the process starting line 319. There are many numbers, sub-steps etc and it is hard to keep track.
-	There are several IAA measure (e.g., Cohen Kappa), why use the percentage of agreement?
-	Please move details on task definition to the main text, this is an important part of the work and should be made more clear.
-	Line 431: why limit the prompt design to C2? The results in figure 3 shows numbers for all criteria, making that sentence confusing.
-	I suggest adding results for un-finetuned Llama 2. The great effectiveness it is showing compared to GPT-4o is surprising and contradicting with existing literature comparing closed models to Llama 2.

Thank you for your thoughtful review. We have attached the revised version of our paper to the general comment above for your consideration. Additionally, we would like to address each of your concerns in detail below:

1/ To improve clarity, we have revised the opening paragraph of the Dataset Description Section to offer a more detailed explanation of the dataset. Furthermore, we have added visualizations in Background Section(Figure 1) and Data Description (Figure 2) Section to better illustrate our approach.

2/Regarding the OCR details, we evaluated a commercial text-from-PDF extractor that includes an OCR pipeline (ABBYY FineReader) during data analysis, but determined that using this extractor resulted in worse performance for the downstream task of relevant text matching compared to using an open-source extractor (PyMuPDF). Therefore, we did not use an OCR tool as part of our experiments. This is mentioned in Appendix E (Limitations). We kept OCR settings in ABBYY FineReader to their defaults (“Thorough recognition”, and targeting the English language only), and provide the processing results as part of our datasets for future researchers interested in using them.

3/ We have replaced the bullet points introducing the mandatory criteria in the Background Section with a visualization (Figure 1). This change integrates the criteria, questions, and examples into a cohesive visual format for improved clarity.

4/ The specific company involved in the annotation process will be disclosed in the camera-ready version of the paper; it is an organization that is both highly professional and specialized in this domain. While the current manuscript already includes extensive information on the annotation process, we would like to emphasize that the annotators were trained using a detailed annotation specification document, which has been submitted alongside the paper. Additionally, Section E.2 ("Contracting and Quality Assurance Details") of Appendix E comprehensively outlines the procedures used to train and test the annotators' knowledge to ensure high-quality results. If there are any additional details you would like us to elaborate on, we would be pleased to provide them.

5/We present the details related to the train/valid/test split in the first paragraph in the Benchmark Experiments Section. 

6/We have taken your suggestions to shorten the Related Works Section into account and relocated the Related Works Section to precede the Conclusion. In the main text, we retained paragraphs specifically addressing the use of AI in analyzing modern slavery statements. Broader related works have been moved to Appendix A, with their key conclusions summarized within the main text for clarity.

7/ We  hope that the revised paragraph ( which used to start with line 250) and the newly added flowchart provide greater clarity regarding the number of documents annotated. Additionally, what is now line 211 has been modified to explicitly state: “The 5,731 statements are associated with over 7,200 entities and 10,000 trademarks across more than 20 industrial sectors.” For clarification, it is important to note that a single statement may cover multiple reporting entities.

8/ We added a new visualization (Figure 2) to the main paper highlighting our process. 

9/ We added Cohen's Kappa results to our IAA score to better account for the likelihood that the annotators agree by chance.

10/ We believe that Figures 1 and 2 now provide clearer insights into the task definition. Additionally, we have moved the two tables from the Additional Results Appendix into the main text to present the full results of our experiments.

11/ We also incorporated your suggestions to bring the two tables with full results from the Additional Results Appendix into the main text, replacing the previous two figures in the Results Section. Additionally, we have modified the text accordingly.

12/ Running a zero-shot experiment with Llama2 (7B) requires computational capabilities beyond our current budget; this is due to the long prompts that are used in the zero-shot setting, which increase inference costs significantly. We added results for Llama3.2 3B for both the zero-shot and the fine-tuned case instead to compare with GPT models. These results showcase how the fine-tuned models greatly outperforms zero-shot approaches, and how Llama3.2 is significantly worse than the GPT models in the zero-shot setting.

summary.value: This paper explores the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify specific actions companies have taken to combat modern slavery and distinguish these from ambiguous corporate statements. To support this analysis, the paper presents a new dataset comprising around 6,000 modern slavery statements sourced from the Australian Modern Slavery Register, with annotations at the sentence level.

strengths.value:
Below, I outline the key strengths of the paper: 

1. The dataset introduced in this paper could prove invaluable for legal professionals, offering a detailed resource for examining modern slavery statements. Furthermore, the annotation guidelines proposed have the potential to be adapted and applied to similar documents across different countries. 
2. The task of distinguishing between specific countermeasures and vague claims addressed by this paper is particularly noteworthy due to the common human difficulty in making such distinctions. The authors demonstrate that Language Models perform reasonably well in this respect, suggesting that these models can be effectively used to support human decision-making processes.

weaknesses.value:
The weaknesses are as follows: 

1. I am concerned about the annotation quality of the dataset. The paper notes that 50 statements were annotated by two expert annotators in lines 240-242, but it lacks details on annotator agreement, the total number of sentences annotated, and other relevant metrics on this smaller set. 
2. The paper does not provide a detailed quantitative and qualitative analysis of Large Language Model (LLM) performance. Specific questions remain unaddressed, such as whether certain words or phrases correlate with LLM outputs or how the distribution of relevant sentences identified by LLMs compares to those identified by annotators. Additionally, it would be useful to know how many different prompts were tested on the LLMs to better understand the models’ responsiveness.

questions.value: I have outlined some questions in the weaknesses section. Additionally, I am curious about the authors' choice not to use traditional metrics such as Fleiss’ Kappa to evaluate inter-annotator agreement.

confidence.description: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

metareview.value:
The paper introduces a manually constructed and annotated dataset designed to analyze modern slavery compliance and countermeasures in corporate text sourced from the Australian Modern Slavery Register. The paper benchmarks language models, including both LLMs (e.g., GPT models) and smaller models (e.g., BERT, DistilBERT), in zero-shot and supervised learning settings. It has been reported that fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot prompting LLMs, underscoring the dataset's value in improving compliance analysis. 

**Some of the strengths of the paper**:
1. The paper addresses a unique and socially important problem: analyzing modern slavery statements to improve corporate compliance and transparency. The dataset and methodology have the potential to significantly impact legal professionals, corporate governance, and broader social accountability.

2. The dataset is extensive, covering a large number of corporate entities (7,270) and multiple years (2019–2023) under the Australian Modern Slavery Act. It provides a valuable resource for examining and distinguishing between specific countermeasures and vague claims in modern slavery statements.

3. The approach and annotation guidelines could be extended to similar problems and datasets in other regions or contexts, broadening its utility beyond Australia.

4. The experiments cover a variety of setups, including different types of LLMs and SLMs in both fine-tuning and zero-shot settings, showcasing the robustness of the evaluation.

**Weaknesses that if addressed can strengthen the paper**:
1. Dataset quality and annotation process: Lack of details on annotator agreement metrics, characteristics of annotators, and their training. Also, missing specific examples of questions or answers used in the annotation process and how these influenced dataset quality.

2. Limited experimental scope and missed opportunities to explore advanced techniques or diverse models: Missing comparisons between zero-shot open and fine-tuned open LLMs. Lack of exploration of advanced techniques like few-shot prompting or chain-of-thought prompting to benchmark closed LLMs.

3. Restricted generalizability and lack of broader impact discussion.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: The overall discussion was relatively good. The concerns raised by reviewer Bg64 (related to dataset annotation quality, training dataset details, and quantitative/qualitative details on LLM performance analysis) have been addressed in subsequent additional experiments and paraphrasing of content. Similar additions were made as per suggestions of reviewer Tmar (concerns were related to annotator agreement metrics, train dataset details, and LLM performance analysis). In response to reviewer Xy2v, the authors have provided detailed additional experimental results partially addressing the concerns related to the annotation process and generalizability on other datasets. All such exchanges led to increase in scores.
